skill.name: canvas-design
skill.description: Use when the agent needs to produce an original visual artifact — poster, art piece, layout, static design — as a .png or .pdf, grounded in a generated design philosophy rather than mimicking an existing artist.
whenToUse: Producing a one-off poster or social card where the user wants real visual design, not a stock template
Creating a brand-adjacent static piece where the philosophy should drive form, color, and composition
Generating a PDF page that needs to read as designed work, with imagery and minimal text functioning together
Turning a written brief into both a design philosophy doc and the visual expression of that philosophy

keyConcepts.explanation: First create a design philosophy as a .md (form, space, color, composition principles), then express it as a .pdf or .png. The two-step split prevents the agent from collapsing into stock layouts.
The philosophy is an aesthetic movement: how form, space, color, and pattern interact. Templates and layouts are explicitly out of scope.
Output composition is dominated by visual elements; text appears only as visual accent. The skill refuses to lean on heavy text blocks to do the design's work.
The skill is explicit about not copying named artists' styles to avoid copyright violations. Compose a philosophy that draws on movements and forms, not signature styles.
Output is constrained to .md (philosophy), .pdf, and .png. Anything dynamic — animation, code, interactive — is a different skill.

apiReference.purpose: Install the canvas-design skill from Anthropic's official skills repo.

gotchas: Skipping the philosophy step produces generic posters; do not collapse the two-step protocol to save time
Avoid naming or imitating specific artists; describe movements, forms, and color systems instead
Text-heavy outputs violate the 90/10 rule and tend to look like slides; if the brief needs text, this is the wrong skill
Static formats only — for animated, dynamic, or interactive output, route to a different skill
User-provided constraints are seeds, not handcuffs; the philosophy should respect them but still take creative direction
